builder_plan.scenario: An assistant chooses the wrong API or sends arguments your product cannot use.
builder_plan.change: Apply the proposed tool-selection or argument-generation change in a sandbox.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current agent with the same tool schemas and task budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct completed actions, invalid calls, retries, latency, and cost per completed task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
summary: It replaces indiscriminate activation of reasoning, RAG, web search, and calculator capabilities on every query with a small Qwen2.5 router (1.5B-14B) making four independent routing decisions via prompt optimization. The cost is router inference overhead, which grows with router capacity and was measured in a separate environment, plus the effort of capability-specific prompt tuning and maintaining labeled routing data. Failures are capability-dependent: false-positive activations waste compute without quality loss, while false negatives on RAG and web search degrade answer quality, and similar classification F1 scores can hide these divergent downstream effects.
rationale: The approach fits a single 24 GB GPU and offers large token and latency savings, but the 127-question evaluation, capability-dependent error profiles, and unquantified router overhead mean the reader must validate the quality-versus-savings trade-off on their own workload before production adoption.
technique: Small-LLM capability router with prompt optimization

claims.statement: It replaces indiscriminate activation of reasoning, RAG, web search, and calculator capabilities on every query with a small Qwen2.5 router (1.5B-14B) making four independent routing decisions via prompt optimization. The cost is router inference overhead, which grows with router capacity and was measured in a separate environment, plus the effort of capability-specific prompt tuning and maintaining labeled routing data. Failures are capability-dependent: false-positive activations waste compute without quality loss, while false negatives on RAG and web search degrade answer quality, and similar classification F1 scores can hide these divergent downstream effects.

A 14B router reduces average downstream token consumption by 68.7% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median latency by 80.5% (9.79s to 1.91s) versus enabling all capabilities, with BERTScore F1 of 0.8408 versus 0.8418 for the all-on baseline.
